business_question: What is the overall campaign subscription rate?
finding: Only 11.3% of contacted clients subscribed to a term deposit.
interpretation: Severe class imbalance (8:1). Models must account for this via class weighting or resampling to avoid predicting 'no' for everyone.

business_question: Which job types have the highest/lowest subscription rates?
finding: Students (31.4%) and retired clients show the highest conversion; blue-collar (6.9%) and services workers the lowest.
interpretation: Students and retirees may have more disposable savings and less financial urgency, making term deposits more attractive. Targeting campaigns toward these segments could improve ROI.

business_question: Does client age influence subscription likelihood?
evidence: Highest conversion band: 66+ (46.9%); subscribed median age 37 vs non-subscribed 38
finding: The 66+ age group has the highest conversion (46.9%). The KDE shows subscribed clients skew slightly older.
interpretation: Younger (18-25) and older (66+) clients convert better than the core working age 36-55 bracket. Younger clients may be in early savings mode; older clients may have capital to deploy. Mid-career clients have more competing financial priorities.

evidence: Highest conversion: illiterate (22.2%); university.degree=13.7% vs basic.4y=10.2%
finding: University degree holders and the 'illiterate' category have the highest conversion rates. There is a general upward trend from basic to higher education.
interpretation: Higher education correlates with higher subscription rates, likely reflecting greater financial literacy and awareness of term deposit benefits.

business_question: Do housing/personal loans or marital status affect subscription?
evidence: housing loan: no=10.9%, yes=11.6%; single marital: 14.0%
finding: Clients without a housing loan convert at nearly double the rate of those with one. Single clients convert slightly higher than married/divorced.
interpretation: Existing debt obligations reduce willingness/ability to lock money in a term deposit. Clients with no housing loan have higher disposable savings.

business_question: Does contact method or contact frequency affect subscription?
finding: Cellular contact yields 14.7% vs telephone 5.2%. Subscription rate drops steeply after the 1st contact and is lowest at high contact counts.
interpretation: Clients reachable by mobile phone are likely more responsive. Repeated calls show diminishing — then negative — returns; persistent calling may cause disengagement. 1-2 contacts is optimal.

business_question: Are certain months or days of week better for campaigns?
evidence: Best month: mar (50.5%), Worst: may (6.4%); Best day: thu (12.1%)
finding: March, September, October and December have the highest conversion rates (>20%), while May has the lowest despite being the highest-volume month. Day-of-week differences are minor (~1 pp spread).
interpretation: The inverse relationship between call volume and conversion in May suggests mass-calling campaigns sacrifice quality. Low-volume months (Mar, Sep-Dec) likely target more qualified leads. Day of week has negligible impact.

business_question: Does previous campaign outcome predict current subscription?
evidence: poutcome=success: 65.1%, nonexistent: 8.8%; previously contacted: 63.8% vs new: 9.3%
finding: Clients who subscribed in a previous campaign convert at 65.1% — nearly 3x the overall rate. Previously contacted clients (63.8%) also outperform never-contacted clients (9.3%).
interpretation: Past behaviour is the strongest single categorical predictor. Retargeting clients with a prior 'success' outcome should be the highest-priority segment for any new campaign.

business_question: Do macro-economic conditions drive subscription likelihood?
finding: Lower employment variation rates and lower Euribor rates are strongly associated with higher subscription rates. Consumer confidence shows a positive relationship.
interpretation: During periods of low interest rates and economic contraction (negative emp_var_rate), clients are more likely to lock savings in term deposits, possibly seeking security. This aligns with the 2008-2012 post-crisis banking context of this dataset.

business_question: Are there multicollinear features that need to be addressed?
evidence: High correlations (|r|>0.7): cons_price_idx/emp_var_rate=0.78; euribor3m/emp_var_rate=0.97; nr_employed/emp_var_rate=0.91; nr_employed/euribor3m=0.95
finding: Strong multicollinearity exists among emp_var_rate, euribor3m, nr_employed, and cons_price_idx — all macro indicators that move together.
interpretation: These collinear features carry redundant information. For linear models, only one or two should be retained (e.g. euribor3m). Tree-based models are less sensitive but feature importance may be diluted.
